stem: A 64-year-old with bipolar I disorder takes lithium 900 mg each night. Following three days of vomiting she develops coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion and diarrhoea. Her creatinine is 180 µmol/L (previously 90). Lithium concentration is 2.5 mmol/L.
options: Continue lithium and add propranolol for the tremor.
Stop lithium, assess ABC and hydration, give appropriate IV fluids and urgently consult toxicology/nephrology.
Give a single activated charcoal dose as definitive treatment.
Give furosemide to force lithium elimination before assessing volume status.
Give an antipsychotic and discharge because confusion is a new manic episode.
explanations: Neurological symptoms and renal impairment indicate lithium toxicity; further doses worsen exposure.
Correct: symptomatic lithium toxicity requires stopping lithium and consideration of enhanced elimination when severe.
Activated charcoal does not effectively adsorb lithium.
Diuresis during dehydration can worsen AKI and toxicity.
Ataxia, GI symptoms and high serum lithium after dehydration indicate toxic encephalopathy.
pearl: Lithium clearance is renal; dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides increase toxicity risk.
pivot: A mild asymptomatic concentration elevation still requires medication/renal review but may not need dialysis.

steps: Hold lithium and interacting drugs, ECG, electrolytes, renal function, serial lithium and neurological checks.
Restore effective volume with IV isotonic fluid if appropriate; monitor sodium and urine output.
Urgent toxicology and nephrology input for severe neurological toxicity, very high lithium or poor clearance; consider haemodialysis criteria.
Medication education, sick-day lithium advice and future level monitoring.
management.safety: Serum level may not correlate perfectly with chronic tissue toxicity; neurological findings matter.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 35-year-old hospitalised for psychosis was started on high-dose haloperidol four days ago. Now temperature is 40°C, there is marked generalized 'lead-pipe' rigidity, autonomic lability and CK 12,000 U/L. Reflexes are not brisk and no clonus is seen.
ask: Which is the BEST initial management?
options: Increase haloperidol to reduce agitation and muscle rigidity.
Treat as serotonin syndrome and give more serotonergic medication.
Stop antipsychotic and initiate emergency supportive and critical-care management with specialist-directed therapy.
Give oral paracetamol alone and review CK in one week.
Wait for MRI brain to prove diagnosis before ceasing antipsychotics.
explanations: Ongoing dopamine blockade worsens probable NMS.
NMS follows dopamine antagonists and features severe rigidity rather than clonus/hyperreflexia.
Correct: NMS risks rhabdomyolysis, renal failure and death.
Hyperthermia from sustained muscle activity and autonomic instability needs urgent medical care.
NMS is primarily clinical and treatment cannot wait for imaging.
pearl: Severe rigidity and high CK following dopamine blockade distinguish NMS from serotonin toxicity with clonus.
pivot: If acute rigidity follows catatonia and no antipsychotic exposure, evaluate malignant catatonia, which shares emergency supportive needs.

steps: Withhold dopamine antagonists and alert psychiatry, medicine and ICU.
Aggressive supportive care with careful fluids, cooling, electrolyte/renal and ECG/CK monitoring.
Specialist review for bromocriptine, dantrolene or ECT in severe/refractory NMS.
Carefully reassess future antipsychotic choice and dosing.
management.safety: Avoid restraints that increase heat production; monitor for rhabdomyolysis and thrombosis.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 28-year-old has had seven months of schizophrenia-spectrum psychotic symptoms. During two months she also met full criteria for major depression, but persecutory delusions and hallucinations persisted for six weeks without any major mood symptoms. Mood episodes have occupied most of the total illness duration.
options: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features because depression occurred.
Schizophrenia because delusions occurred outside mood episodes.
Bipolar I disorder because any psychosis implies prior mania.
Delusional disorder because functioning can sometimes be preserved.
Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
explanations: In psychotic depression, psychosis does not persist for a substantial period outside mood episodes.
Schizophrenia may be considered if mood episodes occupy a minority of the illness, not most.
No manic episode is described.
Prominent hallucinations and mood episodes with broad psychosis are not typical isolated delusional disorder.
Correct: at least two weeks of psychosis without major mood syndrome plus mood episodes during the majority of illness supports schizoaffective disorder.
pearl: The proportion of illness occupied by major mood episodes distinguishes schizoaffective from schizophrenia; psychosis outside mood episodes distinguishes from mood disorder with psychotic features.
pivot: If mood episodes occur only briefly during chronic psychosis, schizophrenia with mood symptoms is more likely.

steps: Document psychotic symptoms, major depressive/manic episodes and fully euthymic intervals.
Psychiatry-led antipsychotic treatment with targeted management of major mood syndrome and relapse supports.
Function, risk, adherence, family engagement and physical-health monitoring.
management.safety: Do not diagnose from one cross-sectional interview; longitudinal collateral is essential.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 39-year-old taking clozapine 350 mg daily has had no bowel movement for six days, increasing abdominal distension and vomiting. HR is 126/min, abdomen is tender and bowel sounds are absent.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Urgent hospital assessment for clozapine-associated gastrointestinal hypomotility/ileus; withhold clozapine pending specialist review.
Advise extra fibre alone and a routine clinic review next week.
Increase clozapine to improve psychotic symptoms before evaluating the abdomen.
Give loperamide to reduce vomiting-related diarrhoea risk.
Reassure because constipation is common and therefore harmless on clozapine.
explanations: Correct: GI hypomotility can progress to obstruction and fatal ischaemia; emergency surgical evaluation is needed.
Severe symptoms may indicate ileus/obstruction where fibre alone can worsen distension.
Clozapine worsens gut hypomotility; escalation is unsafe.
Antimotility drugs worsen obstruction and are not indicated.
High prevalence does not mean safety; red flags demand urgent care.
pearl: Clozapine gastrointestinal hypomotility may be more dangerous than agranulocytosis; actively ask about bowel motions every review.
pivot: Mild constipation without alarm signs requires proactive laxative regimen and monitoring before it progresses.

steps: No stools/flatus, severe pain, distension, vomiting, systemic toxicity; check vitals.
ED/surgery and psychiatry, abdominal imaging and IV fluids as appropriate; review/withhold clozapine.
Surgical or medical decompression according to cause; avoid blind laxatives until obstruction evaluated.
Bowel chart, regular prophylactic laxatives when appropriate, dietary/hydration measures and medication review.
management.safety: Do not use bulking agents when ileus/obstruction is suspected.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 31-year-old has recurrent episodes of palpitations, tremor and intense fear lasting ten minutes. Today she reports similar symptoms plus persistent chest pain and unilateral calf swelling after a long flight. HR 122/min and SpO2 93%.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate approach?
options: Diagnose panic disorder and prescribe an SSRI without further assessment.
Offer breathing exercises as sole treatment, since recurrent attacks prove a functional cause.
Perform urgent assessment for pulmonary embolism and other cardiopulmonary causes before attributing symptoms to panic.
Start long-term benzodiazepine therapy and discharge.
Perform a routine psychiatric personality inventory and review next month.
explanations: Chest pain, hypoxaemia and thromboembolic clues require medical assessment first.
A previous panic diagnosis never excludes an acute medical illness.
Correct: potentially dangerous medical mimics must be excluded using history, vital signs and appropriate investigation.
Sedation can mask deterioration, and long-term benzodiazepines are not preferred panic maintenance therapy.
Immediate physiology and VTE risk take priority.
pearl: Panic symptoms overlap with arrhythmia, PE, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia and stimulant effects.
pivot: If repeated episodes have normal focused medical assessment and expected panic features, CBT and SSRIs may be offered.

steps: ABCDE, ECG, glucose, oxygenation and assess chest pain/leg findings.
PE probability pathway and ECG/troponin when indicated rather than universal testing.
Explain panic physiology, initiate CBT and consider SSRI; avoid reinforcing repeated unnecessary testing.
Return urgently for syncope, persistent chest pain or new breathlessness.
management.safety: Never attribute abnormal vital signs to anxiety by default.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 28-year-old is found unresponsive with RR 5/min, pinpoint pupils and SpO2 75%. A syringe is nearby. A pulse is present; he responds only to painful stimulus.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate treatment?
options: Give flumazenil routinely to reverse opioid-related respiratory depression.
Provide airway/ventilation support and administer naloxone titrated to restoring adequate respiration.
Wait for urine toxicology confirmation before giving any antidote.
Give a sedating antipsychotic for presumed agitation before checking breathing.
Give oral activated charcoal to an unconscious patient without airway protection.
explanations: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with seizure risks, not opioid reversal.
Correct: ventilation is vital; naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression but may wear off before the opioid.
Clinical respiratory depression mandates immediate resuscitation.
Sedation worsens hypoventilation.
High aspiration risk and no role before life-saving airway management.
pearl: In opioid overdose the target is adequate ventilation, not forcing complete alertness at the cost of severe withdrawal.
pivot: If pulseless, initiate CPR and advanced life support while treating likely opioid cause.

steps: Call emergency help, airway manoeuvres, oxygen and bag-mask ventilation; monitor ECG and glucose.
Titrated naloxone IV/IM/intranasal per local pathway; repeat or infuse for long-acting opioids.
Watch for re-sedation, aspiration, pulmonary complications and precipitated withdrawal.
Offer overdose education, take-home naloxone and addiction support after recovery.
management.safety: Do not leave a patient unobserved once naloxone initially works.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A healthy 43-year-old without family history asks for annual mammograms after a friend was diagnosed with breast cancer. She has average baseline risk, no breast symptoms and lives in a country with a population screening start age above 43.
options: Promise annual imaging will prevent all future breast-cancer deaths.
Refuse to discuss screening because she is younger than programme entry age.
Discuss personalised risk, programme guidance, false positives, overdiagnosis and her values before deciding.
Recommend breast MRI annually to every average-risk woman.
Order serum CA15-3 as an alternative cancer screening test.
explanations: Screening can reduce some breast-cancer mortality but has false positives and overdiagnosis; no guarantee exists.
Informed discussion of risk, benefits and harms remains appropriate.
Correct: screening decisions should reflect evidence, age/risk and informed patient preference.
MRI is generally reserved for selected high-risk situations and increases false positives.
Tumour markers do not replace validated breast screening.
pearl: Population screening depends on net benefit in an age/risk group; earlier testing can increase harms without comparable benefit.
pivot: A pathogenic high-risk mutation or strong pedigree requires formal risk assessment and earlier tailored surveillance.

steps: Concerns, symptoms, family history, previous breast findings and expectations.
Absolute potential benefits, false positives, unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis; compare local screening intervals.
Shared plan and breast-awareness advice, with diagnostic imaging if new symptoms appear.
Reassess as age or risk changes.
management.safety: Never call a symptomatic breast lump 'screening'; it requires diagnostic assessment.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 46-year-old after a fall has mild head injury and is repeatedly asking the same questions. He insists on leaving ED while vomiting twice and cannot explain the danger of intracranial bleeding. GCS is 14.
options: Accept refusal solely because he can verbally say 'no'.
Restrain indefinitely without assessing capacity or reviewing least-restrictive measures.
Assess decision-specific capacity, treat reversible causes and use appropriate emergency care authority if he lacks capacity.
Obtain a family signature to override him without any evaluation.
Tell him that all refusal is illegal after an injury.
explanations: Decision-making capacity includes understanding and appreciation, not just expressing a preference.
Restriction requires legal/clinical justification and proportionate reassessment.
Correct: memory impairment may undermine appreciation of immediate risk; prioritise safety within local law.
Relatives do not automatically replace capable adult decisions, and incapacity must be established.
Capable adults can refuse care; the decision hinges on actual capacity and urgent risks.
pearl: Capacity is decision- and time-specific, not equivalent to orientation or GCS alone.
pivot: A patient who accurately understands and weighs risks may retain capacity even when declining clinician advice.

steps: Explain CT/observation indications, risks of intracranial bleed and alternatives; ask teach-back.
Manage pain, nausea and possible intoxication; obtain CT/head injury assessment as required.
If lacks capacity and serious imminent harm, use legally authorised least-restrictive emergency care.
Specific deficits, rationale, actions and reassessment.
management.safety: Never equate an unwise decision with incapacity.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 52-year-old with diabetes and BP 146/88 mmHg has eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m² and urine albumin:creatinine ratio 47 mg/mmol on two samples. K is 4.5 mmol/L. He has no contraindication to ACE inhibitors.
ask: Which long-term kidney-protective action is MOST appropriate?
options: Use ACE inhibitor or ARB with kidney function/potassium monitoring and assess SGLT2 inhibitor eligibility.
Avoid all BP drugs until eGFR falls below 30.
Give dual ACE inhibitor plus ARB routinely for stronger proteinuria reduction.
Give NSAIDs regularly to lower kidney inflammation.
Stop diabetic control because the main problem is albuminuria.
explanations: Correct: albuminuric diabetic CKD benefits from RAAS blockade and often SGLT2 inhibition if eligible.
Early blood pressure and kidney protection reduces progression risk.
Dual RAAS blockade increases AKI and hyperkalaemia risk without acceptable benefit.
NSAIDs increase nephrotoxicity and BP risks.
Glucose and cardiovascular risk control remain essential.
pearl: Albuminuric CKD warrants RAAS blockade and cardiorenal risk modification, not just creatinine monitoring.
pivot: Marked hyperkalaemia, bilateral renal artery stenosis or pregnancy changes ACE/ARB suitability.

steps: Trend eGFR/ACR over at least three months, BP and reversible causes.
Titrate ACE/ARB if appropriate, check K/creatinine 1–2 weeks after changes; consider SGLT2 therapy by eGFR and indications.
BP targets, diabetes, statin, smoking and avoidance of nephrotoxins.
Rapid decline, heavy proteinuria, resistant hypertension or difficult electrolytes merit nephrology.
management.safety: Monitor initial creatinine rise and potassium; don't automatically stop protective therapy after minor predictable changes.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 33-year-old paramedic develops intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of driving near an accident scene, irritability and hypervigilance three months after a traumatic rescue. Symptoms impair work. He has no psychosis or substance misuse.
ask: Which ongoing treatment is BEST supported?
options: Use trauma-focused psychological treatment such as trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, considering an SSRI if indicated.
Offer prolonged benzodiazepine monotherapy to erase traumatic memory.
Recommend avoiding all reminders indefinitely to prevent physiological stress.
Start antipsychotic monotherapy for all nightmares and hypervigilance.
Diagnose adjustment disorder because PTSD requires psychosis.
explanations: Correct: evidence-based trauma-focused therapy is a first-line PTSD intervention.
Long-term benzodiazepines have dependence and impaired recovery risks and are not first-line PTSD therapy.
Avoidance maintains PTSD symptoms; therapy addresses fear learning safely.
Antipsychotics are not universal first-line PTSD treatment.
PTSD does not require psychosis and includes intrusion, avoidance, cognition/mood and arousal symptoms.
pearl: PTSD involves persistent intrusion, avoidance, mood/cognition changes and hyperarousal after trauma; first-line care is trauma-focused therapy.
pivot: Symptoms resolving within a few days without functional impairment may represent a normal acute stress response.

steps: Trauma symptoms, duration, function, depression, substance use and suicidality.
Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with informed consent and pacing; consider SSRIs when therapy unavailable/declined or comorbidity warrants.
Sleep, work accommodations, social supports and relapse monitoring.
Track outcomes and safety; avoid routine long-term benzodiazepines.
management.safety: Do not force detailed trauma recounting during an unstable or unsafe period.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.
